cells.name: Modernism
cells.description: Art that rejects the past as a model for the present. Tate names the principles: a rejection of history and of conservative values such as realistic depiction, innovation and experiment with form, tending to abstraction, and an emphasis on materials, techniques and processes. Modernist work draws attention to how it was made and what it was made from, and it gave up absolute originality for collage, reprise, rewriting, recapitulation and parody. Tate applies the term to a succession of movements that critics and historians have identified, from Courbet's realism to the abstraction of the 1960s, when Clement Greenberg's theory of modernist painting narrowed it and postmodernism formed against it.

maps.explanation: Tate defines modernism as a broad movement in Western art, architecture and design, and Wikipedia names the visual arts among its fields.
Wikipedia's first sentence names literature among the fields the movement covers.
Tate defines modernism as a broad movement in Western art, architecture and design.

questions: Abstract art is a root and no source checked puts it here. Its own Wikipedia article, Tate's abstract art page and Wikidata all stop short of placing abstract art under modernism, and Wikidata files it under modern art instead. Tate's modernism page says only that the succession culminates in abstract art, which could mean that abstract art is inside modernism or that modernism ends where abstract art begins. Place it here once a source says abstract art is inside modernism.

Constructivism is a root because the only sentence in the sources checked says socialist realism began to oust modernism in the Soviet Union, which had previously endorsed Russian Futurism and Constructivism. That implies Constructivism is part of modernism without saying so.

This pass checked Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, Symbolism, Fluxus, Arte Povera, Gutai, CoBrA, Nouveau Réalisme and the School of Paris against their own pages, Tate, Wikidata and Getty AAT, and none of those sources places them under modernism. They stay roots.

Their own articles call Minimalism, Pop art, Conceptual art and Land art reactions against modernism, so none of them is a child here, even though the Modernism article lists Minimalism and Pop art among late twentieth-century modernist movements.

This cell is on the writing and design maps because its sources name literature, architecture and design, but the art pass placed every child so far. A writing pass and a design pass would each choose their own children.
Modernism is used both as a direction and as a name for a period of roughly 1860 to 1970. Which sense does a reader browsing this cell expect, and does the scope need to say which one it means?

Getty AAT has no concept for modernism as a parent. The records for Dada, Cubist, Surrealist, Constructivist, Expressionist, Futurist and Fauve each give a guide term in angle brackets as their only broader concept, a term that sorts by nation and period, so AAT contributes no children here.

cells.name: Expressionism
cells.description: A modernist movement that began in northern Europe around 1900 and shows the world entirely from a subjective position, distorting it for emotional effect. It runs across painting, poetry, drama, film and architecture, with Die Brücke and Der Blaue Reiter as its German painting groups. The distortion is a claim about what is real.

maps.explanation: A named style or movement in the visual arts.
The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.

broader.explanation: Its own article opens by calling Expressionism a modernist movement in poetry and painting, beginning in northern Europe around 1900.

cells.name: Fauvism
cells.description: The short-lived French movement of about 1905 to 1908 in which colour was freed from description. Paint is laid in unmixed saturated areas, drawing is summary, and the colour of a shadow or a face is chosen for the picture rather than for the subject. Matisse, Derain and Vlaminck worked it out at Collioure and L'Estaque.

maps.explanation: A movement in painting with a named body of work.

broader.explanation: Tate's page for Fauvism calls it one of the first avant-garde modernist movements of the twentieth century.

cells.name: Futurism
cells.description: An Italian movement launched by Marinetti's manifesto of 1909, which glorified speed, machinery, youth and violence and demanded that the past be swept away. Boccioni, Balla, Severini and Carrà worked out a painting and sculpture of simultaneous motion, and the movement extended into poetry, typography, music, clothing and cooking. Its politics turned towards Fascism, which is part of its record.

maps.explanation: A named style or movement in the visual arts.
The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.
The movement worked in design as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.

broader.explanation: Tate counts Futurism among modernist movements, and says it was exceptionally vehement in denouncing the past.

cells.name: Cubism
cells.description: Painting and sculpture from about 1908, begun by Braque and Picasso, that shows several sides of an object at once on a flat picture plane. Its analytic phase fractures form; its synthetic phase from 1912 builds with collage and added materials.

maps.explanation: A movement in painting and sculpture.

broader.explanation: Neither Tate's page for Cubism nor the Wikipedia article calls Cubism modernist. Wikidata files cubism as part of modernism.

relations.label: engaged with
relations.explanation: Der Blaue Reiter exhibited and discussed Cubist work; the two avant-gardes read each other closely before 1914.

cells.name: American Modernism
cells.description: The American turn to modernist form from about 1900 through the mid-century, across painting, photography, writing and architecture. The 1913 Armory Show and Stieglitz's 291 gallery brought European modernism into the argument, and O'Keeffe, Dove, Demuth and Hartley made an American version of it. Its recurring question is what an American modern art would owe Europe.

maps.explanation: A named style or movement in the visual arts.
The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.

broader.explanation: Wikidata files American modernism as a subclass of modernism.

cells.name: International Typographic Style
cells.description: The Swiss graphic design of the 1950s onward: an underlying grid, asymmetric layout, sans-serif type set flush left and ragged right, objective photography, and information organised so the structure is visible. It was taught in Basel and Zurich and became standard for signage, timetables and corporate systems.

maps.explanation: A movement in graphic design with a named body of work and a teaching lineage.
Design languages take the grid, the type discipline and the restrained signal colour from it.

broader.explanation: Its own article calls the style a modernist graphic movement, and places it within the modernist movement.

questions: Getty AAT Styles and Periods has no concept for this movement, so the cell cites Wikipedia and Wikidata instead. Revisit if an AAT term is added.

cells.name: Surrealism
cells.description: A movement of poets and artists centred on Paris from the 1920s to the 1940s, defined by André Breton's 1924 manifesto as psychic automatism. Automatic writing and drawing, dream imagery, and ordinary objects placed in impossible relationships are its working methods, in text and in image alike.

maps.explanation: A movement in painting, object and film.
Founded by a poet with a literary manifesto; Surrealist prose and poetry are the movement's own.

broader.explanation: Surrealism's own Tate page does not call Surrealism modernist. The Modernism article says that in the painting of the 1920s and 1930s Surrealism was among the movements that defined modernism, and that the public came to regard Surrealism as the most extreme form of modernism.

relations.label: anticipated by
relations.explanation: Breton's Anthology of Black Humour (1940) includes Lewis Carroll, claiming nonsense for Surrealism's prehistory.

cells.name: Dada
cells.description: An international movement begun in Zurich in 1916 as a response to the war and to the society that produced it, rejecting art's existing forms in favour of an anti-art of chance, collage, nonsense and provocation. It spread to Berlin, Hanover, Cologne, Paris and New York, each centre taking it differently. Its refusals became the working methods of most of what followed.

maps.explanation: A named style or movement in the visual arts.
The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.

broader.explanation: Dada's own article does not call Dada modernist. The Modernism article names Dada among the movements that defined modernism in the painting of the 1920s and 1930s.

cells.name: Bauhaus
cells.description: The German school of 1919 to 1933 and the work that came out of it. A preliminary course in material and colour, workshops that joined craft to industrial production, geometric form, primary colour and sans-serif type. Its output covers weaving, furniture, photography, typography and light studies.

maps.explanation: A school and a movement with a large documented body of work.
Its workshops produced design for manufacture, and design languages take their geometry and colour discipline from it.

broader.explanation: Bauhaus's own article goes no further than calling the Bauhaus style one of the most influential currents in modernist architecture. The Modernism article names it among the movements that defined modernism in the painting of the 1920s and 1930s.
